## Definition
**Nerve conduction** is the propagation of electrical signals (**action potentials**) along the membranes of neurons — a key example of **bioelectricity**, the electrical phenomena generated by living cells. It rests on the same physics as circuits: charge, [[Voltage|voltage]], the [[ElectricField|electric field]], and Coulomb forces, applied to ion movement across a cell membrane.

## Key Points
- A neuron has dendrites (receive signals), an axon (transmits), and synapses (transfer signals between cells).
- The membrane maintains unequal Na⁺/K⁺/Cl⁻ concentrations, giving a **resting potential** of ≈ −90 mV (inside negative). The thin (~8 nm) membrane sustains a large field, E = V/d ≈ 11 MV/m.
- Active transport (the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) spends ~25% of cellular ATP to keep these gradients against diffusion.
- An **action potential** is a voltage pulse: a permeability change lets Na⁺ flood in (**depolarization**), then K⁺ flows out (**repolarization**), and the pulse spreads to neighboring membrane.
- **Myelin** sheaths insulate axon segments separated by nodes of Ranvier; signals jump node-to-node (**saltatory conduction**), reaching ~100 m/s vs ~1 m/s in unmyelinated fibers, with much lower energy cost. Myelin loss (multiple sclerosis) impairs conduction.
- The heart's coordinated depolarization is recorded by an **electrocardiogram (ECG/EKG)**: the P wave (atrial depolarization), QRS complex (ventricular depolarization), and T wave (ventricular repolarization); Lead II runs right arm to left leg.

## Equations
- E = V / d  (membrane field; d ≈ 8 nm → E ≈ 11 MV/m)
